questions.question: Explain how tilted strata produce asymmetrical ridges, defining dip, dip slope and scarp slope, and stating why the two slopes differ in steepness.
questions.expected_answer: Strata are laid down horizontally but are tilted by crustal movements — compression and folding, unequal uplift, or the sagging and arching of basins. The dip is the angle between a tilted layer and the horizontal. When differential erosion attacks tilted layers of unequal strength, soft layers are excavated into valleys and resistant layers survive as ridges, but the ridge is asymmetrical because its two sides obey different rules. The dip slope follows the tilted upper surface of the resistant layer itself, so it is gentle and its angle matches the dip of the rock — one hard layer stays underfoot all the way down. The scarp slope cuts across the broken edges of the strata, exposing soft layers beneath the truncated resistant band; the soft layers erode quickly and undermine the hard band, which holds a steep, often cliffed face. The contrast is between a protected layer surface and a cut edge: dip follows one layer, scarp cuts across many.

questions.question: Classify cuesta, homoclinal ridge and hogsback by dip angle with South African examples, and describe the geometry of cuesta basins and cuesta domes including the facing directions of their slopes.
questions.expected_answer: The three ridges are one landform at increasing dip. Strata dipping gently, up to about 25 degrees, form a cuesta: a strongly asymmetrical ridge with a long gentle dip slope and a short steep scarp. Dips of roughly 25 to 45 degrees form a homoclinal ridge, still asymmetrical but narrower and sharper — the Magaliesberg quartzite ridge past Pretoria and Rustenburg is the textbook example. Beyond about 45 degrees, with layers standing nearly on end, both sides cut across the strata at similar steep angles and the ridge becomes a narrow, near-symmetrical hogsback, as above the Eastern Cape village of Hogsback. The trend is that steeper dip narrows the ridge and equalises its slopes. In a cuesta basin the strata sag toward a centre, so erosion leaves concentric resistant ridges whose dip slopes face inward and scarp slopes face outward; water entering the tilted aquifers at the rim collects under pressure beneath the centre, allowing artesian boreholes. In a cuesta dome the strata arch over a centre and dip away from it, so dip slopes face outward and scarps face inward across the eroded core — the Vredefort Dome's concentric ridges are the famous South African case. In both, the dip slope faces the way the layers lean downward.

questions.question: Describe how tilted-strata landscapes are identified and analysed on a 1:50 000 map, including gradient and vertical exaggeration calculations, and how people use such landscapes.
questions.expected_answer: Asymmetry is the map signature: a cuesta or homoclinal ridge shows contours tightly crowded on the scarp side of the crest and widely spaced on the dip side, while a hogsback shows crowding on both sides of a narrow crest, and concentric ring patterns suggest a basin or dome. The impression is confirmed numerically with a gradient on each side: with a crest at 1 500 metres and the 1 300-metre contour 400 metres away on the north but 2 000 metres away on the south, the north gradient is 200 over 400 or 1 in 2 and the south is 200 over 2 000 or 1 in 10, so the north is the scarp and the strata dip south, toward the gentle side. A cross-section perpendicular to the crest shows the right-angled-triangle profile; with a vertical scale of 1 centimetre to 100 metres, which is 1:10 000, against the 1:50 000 horizontal scale the vertical exaggeration is 50 000 divided by 10 000, which is 5 times. People fit themselves to the structure: farms, plantations and settlement occupy the gentle dip slopes, roads, railways and towns follow the strike valleys between ridges, scarp faces stay wild, and crossings concentrate where rivers have cut poorts through the resistant crest, as at the Hartbeespoort gap in the Magaliesberg.
